entries.description: Predicts elapsed time and trap speed from flywheel HP and vehicle weight.
Converts 1/8 mile elapsed time to estimated 1/4 mile ET using the standard 1.569× multiplier.
Reports a 3D CG coordinate and its distance from the vehicle reference origin. Use consistent vehicle coordinate references for x, y and z.
Compressor RPM from engine RPM and pulley sizes.

Shows approximate saturated/static R-134a pressure from a published pressure-temperature table. This is NOT an operating low/high-side diagnostic chart; running pressures depend on system design, charge, airflow, compressor speed, and evaporator/condenser conditions.
Provides a simple diagnostic target rather than pretending to predict exact vent temperature. A common rule-of-thumb is roughly 35–55°F below ambient under favorable conditions.
Gearhead Labs Premium unlocks AC Power Factor — the real-power fraction behind alternator/stator loading and AC accessory circuit analysis.

Rear Load Transfer = Weight × CG Height × Acceleration G ÷ Wheelbase. Hard acceleration shifts weight onto the rear tires — real, useful extra grip for a rear-drive launch, which is exactly why launching hard actually helps rear-wheel-drive traction rather than just spinning the tires.

Inside Angle = arctan[Wheelbase ÷ (Turn Radius − Wheelbase÷2)]. Proper Ackermann geometry steers the inside front wheel MORE sharply than the outside wheel in a turn, since the inside wheel follows a tighter-radius arc — this finds that correct inside-wheel angle for a given turn.

Ideal Ackermann angle to eliminate tire scrub in turns — the static geometry target from wheelbase and track width alone. For the actual inside-wheel steering angle needed at a specific turn radius, use Ackermann Geometry instead.

entries.definition: Steering geometry in which the inside front wheel turns more than the outside so both follow circles about a common centre.

entries.description: Combined Weight = Tow Vehicle Weight + Trailer Weight. The real total weight the drivetrain, brakes, and chassis actually have to manage together — the figure to check directly against GCWR.
Fractions are reduced; nearest-fraction tools use 1/64-inch increments.
Use the free ET & MPH Prediction calculator for a quick quarter-mile estimate. Premium’s Advanced ET Prediction refines it with the extra variables that actually move the number.

Front Aero Balance = Front Aero Load ÷ (Front Aero Load + Rear Aero Load). How a car’s total downforce is actually split between the front and rear axles — a mismatch between this aero balance and the car’s mechanical balance is a common source of speed-sensitive handling behavior.
Calculates the actual front/rear downforce split and compares it directly with the mechanical front weight/CG percentage. No arbitrary 60/40 weighting is applied.

Downforce = ½ × Air Density × Downforce Coefficient × Frontal Area × Speed². Real, usable extra vertical tire loading generated purely by airflow — unlike mechanical grip, downforce costs nothing in ride comfort but only exists at speed.

Drag = ½ × Air Density × Drag Coefficient × Frontal Area × Speed². The real force air resistance exerts on a vehicle — growing with the SQUARE of speed, which is why aero drag becomes the dominant resistance force at highway speed and above.

Aero Power = Drag Force × Speed ÷ 375. The actual horsepower an engine has to dedicate purely to pushing through aerodynamic drag at a given speed — separate from (and in addition to) power needed for rolling resistance and grade.

Lift = ½ × Air Density × Lift Coefficient × Frontal Area × Speed². Unwanted upward aerodynamic force that REDUCES effective tire loading at speed — many production car body shapes generate some lift without dedicated aero aids to counteract it.
AFR = Lambda × Stoichiometric AFR. Converts a lambda sensor reading (fuel-independent) into the actual air/fuel ratio for whatever fuel’s stoich value is used.
Convert between Air/Fuel Ratio and Lambda for any fuel type. λ 1.0 = lean. λ = 1.0 = stoichiometric.

Calculates moist-air density from temperature, pressure and relative humidity. For a direct cross-check against Density Altitude, use the SAME station pressure used by the DA calculation (not the altimeter setting). Result is in lb/ft³ (pound-mass per cubic foot). Water vapor is less dense than dry air, so humidity slightly lowers density at fixed temperature and pressure.
Minimum filter face area to keep velocity under 450 ft/min (no restriction).
Air Mass = Fuel Mass × AFR. The mass of air an engine actually consumed alongside a known fuel mass, given the air/fuel ratio it was running — the reverse of the usual AFR calculation.

Efficiency = 1 - (1 / Compression Ratio^0.4). The same idealized air-standard Otto cycle relationship used in engineering thermodynamics courses — a theoretical ceiling, not a real engine’s actual measured efficiency.
Uses estimated air mass flow, AFR and BSFC to estimate power. This is explicitly an estimate; cylinder-head flow alone does not guarantee engine power.
Uses displacement, RPM, cycle type and VE to estimate engine volume flow. A pressure-ratio adjustment gives an ambient-equivalent volume for boosted applications.

Required Capacity = Vehicle Electrical Load + Reserve Load. A simple sizing target for an alternator upgrade — covering the vehicle’s actual continuous electrical load plus a reserve margin for accessories and battery charging headroom.
Alternator RPM = Engine RPM × (Crank Pulley OD / Alt Pulley OD). Alternators typically need 1,500+ RPM to charge.

entries.definition: The share of the front weight transfer under braking that the suspension geometry carries through the links instead of the springs, given as a percentage.

entries.description: Simplified anti-dive estimate using front brake-force share and instant-center height. Full suspension anti-dive requires the actual side-view suspension geometry and instant-center location.

entries.definition: The share of the rear weight transfer under acceleration that the suspension geometry carries through the links instead of the springs, given as a percentage.

entries.description: Gearhead Labs Premium unlocks Anti-Squat from Link Coordinates — builds the Instant Center Height that the Free Anti-Squat % calculator takes as a direct input, from actual suspension link geometry.

Simplified anti-squat percentage from instant-center height and center-of-gravity height. 100% means the anti-squat line reaches the CG height at the reference wheelbase. Full four-link design also requires link coordinates and force-line geometry.

inputs: Instant Center Height at Reference Wheelbase

entries.description: Idealized angle = atan(lowest-point height / horizontal offset from tire contact patch). This assumes a single lowest point front and rear and ignores tire deflection, sidewall bulge and body panel shape between that point and the tire — a bumper lip or tow hook can reduce the real usable angle below this figure.
Compares your current loan payment to a refinanced rate over the remaining term. Refinancing makes the most sense when rates have dropped or your credit has improved since the original loan.

Gearhead Labs Premium unlocks Axle Shaft Torque Capacity — the same shaft-torsion strength limit as Driveshaft Torque Capacity, framed the way axle specs are quoted: yield torque and safe working torque after a safety factor.
Researched unit conversion / shop math tool from the Gearhead Labs encyclopedia.

Simple pressure-ratio estimate only. This is NOT SAE J1349 and does not account for temperature, humidity, friction, or engine-specific behavior. Use the Dyno Correction calculator for a standards-based correction.
Capacity = Load Current × Runtime. The amp-hour capacity needed to run a given continuous load (a dash cam, an alarm, a winch standby draw) for a target duration without external charging.
Effective CCA drops about 1% per degree below 32°F.
Gearhead Labs Premium unlocks Battery Pack Heat Balance — pack heat, steady and transient temperature against the coolant, and the continuous current to a limit.
Deflection = (Load × Length³) ÷ (48 × Elastic Modulus × Moment of Inertia). Models a simply-supported beam with a single load at its center — a bracket, crossmember, or roll bar spanning two mounts.
Gearhead Labs Premium unlocks Bearing Defect Frequency — BPFO, BPFI, ball spin and cage frequencies from bearing geometry.
Gearhead Labs Premium unlocks Bearing Journal Surface Speed — the velocity term every bearing PV and oil-film check depends on.
Basic ISO 281 rating life: L10 = (C/P)^p million revolutions; p=3 for ball bearings and 10/3 for roller bearings. Hours = L10×10⁶/(60×RPM). This is nominal L10 life, not a guarantee.

Gearhead Labs Premium unlocks the Bearing Preload Calculator — the same torque-to-clamp-force method as the Free Bolt Torque Spec calculator, applied to a preload/spindle nut instead of a structural bolt.
L = 2C + π(D1+D2)/2 + (D1−D2)²/4C, where C is center-to-center distance. Useful for serpentine belts, accessory drives, or custom pulley setups.
Gearhead Labs Premium unlocks Bend Deduction — outside setback, bend deduction and flat blank length.
Gearhead Labs Premium unlocks Bend K-Factor — the neutral-axis K-factor measured from a test bend.
Bending stress = Bending Moment ÷ Section Modulus. The peak fiber stress at the outer surface of a beam or bracket under a bending load.
Gearhead Labs Premium unlocks the Bernoulli Equation calculator — solve for pressure change across a fluid-line transition in elevation, diameter, or velocity.
Gearhead Labs Premium unlocks Blind Hole Depth — tapped depth, drill depth and point allowance for a blind tapped hole.
For a four-stroke engine, BMEP (psi) = 150.8 × torque (lb-ft) ÷ displacement (ci). BMEP is a normalized performance metric, not actual cylinder pressure.

Converts bolt-to-bolt measurement to Pitch Circle Diameter (PCD). Measure across opposing bolts for even-lug wheels, adjacent bolts for odd-lug.
Gearhead Labs Premium unlocks Bolt Preload from Torque — clamp force, preload stress and percent of proof from a tightening torque.
Gearhead Labs Premium unlocks Bolt Shear Capacity — single or double shear through the shank or the threads.

Rod bolts and head studs are often torqued using the stretch method instead of torque wrench alone — more accurate because it directly measures the fastener's elongation, independent of thread friction variance. The loaded plain shank and the loaded thread stretch in series: clamp load = E × stretch ÷ (shank length ÷ shank area + thread length ÷ tensile stress area), E = 29,000,000 psi (steel). Thread beyond the nut carries no load and does not stretch. Thread stress = load ÷ tensile stress area; shank stress = load ÷ shank area. Thread standard: UN uses A_t = π/4 (d − 0.9743/n)² (ASME B1.1, n threads per inch); ISO uses A_s = π/4 (d − 0.9382 P)² (ISO 898-1, P the pitch). An ISO thread is typed in millimetres in both unit systems; threads per inch and pitch are never converted into each other.

inputs: Bolt Length, under head to end (in)
Nominal (Major) Diameter (in; an ISO diameter is mm ÷ 25.4)
Threads per Inch (ISO: 25.4 ÷ pitch in mm)

entries.description: Gearhead Labs Premium unlocks Bolt Tensile Capacity — tensile stress area, proof and ultimate loads for UN or ISO metric threads.

Torque = K × Diameter × Clamp Load, where K ≈ 0.20 dry, 0.15 lubricated. Clamp load target is typically 75% of the bolt's proof load; proof load = proof strength × the tensile stress area of the thread entered. Proof strength by grade and size: SAE J429 Grade 2 55 ksi from 1/4 to 3/4 in and 33 ksi over 3/4 to 1-1/2 in (the 1/4–3/4 in value applies to bolts 6 in and shorter; longer ones are Grade 1, not offered here), Grade 5 85 ksi to 1 in and 74 ksi over 1 to 1-1/2 in, Grade 8 120 ksi from 1/4 to 1-1/2 in; ISO 898-1 class 8.8 580 MPa from M5 to M16 and 600 MPa above, to M39, class 10.9 830 MPa from M5 to M39. Always use lubricated values for stainless to prevent galling. Thread standard: UN uses A_t = π/4 (d − 0.9743/n)² (ASME B1.1, n threads per inch); ISO uses A_s = π/4 (d − 0.9382 P)² (ISO 898-1, P the pitch). An ISO thread is typed in millimetres in both unit systems; threads per inch and pitch are never converted into each other.

inputs: Nominal (Major) Diameter (in; an ISO diameter is mm ÷ 25.4)
Threads per Inch (ISO: 25.4 ÷ pitch in mm)

entries.description: Effective CR under boost = Static CR × (Boost + Atm) / Atm. Know this to avoid detonation — pump gas typically maxes at ~165 psi cylinder pressure.
Estimates boost pressure needed assuming linear relationship between boost and power. Actual results vary with VE, intercooler efficiency, and fuel.
Over-square (bore > stroke) = high-revving, top-end power. Under-square (stroke > bore) = torque, low RPM. Square = balanced.

entries.definition: Cylinder bore divided by piston stroke. Above 1 the engine is called oversquare, below 1 undersquare.

related.note: The rod/stroke ratio compares the connecting rod length, not the bore, with the stroke.

entries.description: Vehicle Dynamics mode computes the ideal bias for your car from weight distribution, CG height, wheelbase and target deceleration, accounting for weight transfer under braking. Measured Force mode checks the bias of forces you already have from an existing proportioning setup. Most performance cars land near 60-65% front, but the correct number depends on your specific weight distribution and CG height, not a universal rule.
Dynamic front weight under braking determines ideal brake bias. As deceleration increases, weight shifts forward, requiring more front braking force. Most road cars: 60–68% front.

Clamp force = hydraulic line pressure × total caliper piston area. Enter piston bore diameter and piston count per caliper — most caliper spec sheets list bore diameter, not area directly. Feed the result into Brake Torque for the next step in the brake chain.

Starting point for trailer brake controller gain. Always fine-tune with the manual override lever: brakes should engage firmly without locking up or being too soft — test at low speed before towing on the road.

Gearhead Labs Premium unlocks Brake Duct CFM — the same sensible-heat airflow formula behind the Free Electric Fan CFM Requirement calculator, sized for a brake cooling duct’s heat-rejection target instead of a radiator’s.
Use the free Brake Torque calculator to establish the baseline. Premium’s Brake Energy analyzes the complete thermal workflow alongside Brake Rotor Temp Rise and Brake Heat per Stop.

Gearhead Labs Premium unlocks Brake Fade Prediction — steps a full braking session stop-by-stop with cooling between stops against your pad’s fade-onset spec, well beyond the existing Energy per Stop calculator’s single-number average.

Gearhead Labs Premium unlocks Brake Fluid Boiling Margin — how much headroom is left between your fluid’s own boiling-point spec and its estimated temperature, with no existing calculator for this today.
Use the free Brake Torque calculator to establish the baseline. Premium’s Brake Heat per Stop completes the thermal workflow alongside Brake Energy and Brake Rotor Temp Rise.
Hydraulic force multiplication is the caliper piston area divided by master-cylinder piston area.

entries.definition: The constant pressure that, acting on the pistons over each power stroke, would give the engine's measured brake (output) torque. It compares torque per unit displacement between engines of different sizes.

related.note: IMEP is the indicated (in-cylinder) value; BMEP is what remains at the crankshaft.

entries.description: Simplified pedal-force estimate from required hydraulic force, pedal ratio and hydraulic multiplication.
Simplified pedal-force estimate from required hydraulic force, pedal ratio and hydraulic multiplication.

Gearhead Labs Premium unlocks Brake Rotor Sizing — the physical effective-radius and minimum-diameter a rotor needs to hit a target torque at a given clamp force, distinct from the existing thermal Rotor Heat/Temperature-Rise calculators.
Use the free Brake Torque calculator to establish the baseline. Premium’s Brake Rotor Temp Rise analyzes the complete thermal picture — rotor temp, energy and fade, together.

Estimates rotor temperature rise from the kinetic energy absorbed by the rotor. Energy is converted from ft-lbf to BTU before dividing by rotor mass and specific heat. This is an idealized single-event estimate; real braking distributes heat into pads, caliper, hub, air, and other rotors.
BSFC = Fuel Flow (lb/hr) / HP. Naturally aspirated gas engines: 0.45–0.55 lb/hp-hr. Forced induction: 0.55–0.65.

Efficiency = Brake Power ÷ Fuel Energy Input Rate. The real-world measure of how much of the fuel’s energy an engine actually converts to usable power at the crank, expressed in the same power-equivalent units on both sides.

Brake torque = clamp force × pad friction coefficient × effective rotor radius. Get clamp force from the Clamp Force calculator, then use this to size or compare rotors and pads. Feed the result into Braking Distance alongside vehicle weight and tire grip to check total stopping performance.

Braking distance from speed, tire friction and road grade, plus driver reaction distance for a real-world total stopping distance. Average reaction time is about 0.75 sec; impaired or distracted drivers can be 1.5+ sec.

Front Load Transfer = Weight × CG Height × Braking G ÷ Wheelbase. Hard braking shifts real weight onto the front tires (and off the rear) — exactly why front brakes do the majority of the stopping work and are sized larger than rears on almost every vehicle.
In bracket racing, running quicker than your dial-in is a "breakout" — an automatic loss, even if you'd have won on a stripe. This is the fundamental risk/reward of bracket racing dial-ins.
Idealized breakover angle = 2 × atan(2 × ground clearance / wheelbase). This assumes the lowest point is at the wheelbase midpoint and ignores tire deflection and body geometry.

Researched unit conversion / shop math tool from the Gearhead Labs encyclopedia.
Track spending against your build budget by category. Enter running totals for each category to see how much budget remains.

entries.definition: The change of toe as the suspension moves up and down, from the steering linkage not following the suspension arcs.

entries.description: Gearhead Labs Premium unlocks the Bump Steer Curve — a five-checkpoint version of the Free Bump Steer Rate calculator that reveals whether the toe curve is linear or progressive across the full stroke.

Bump steer is unwanted toe change as the suspension moves through travel — caused by tie rod end not matching the suspension's arc. Target: under 0.02 in/in of travel. Excess bump steer causes unpredictable handling over bumps and curbs.
Gearhead Labs Premium unlocks Bump Stop Rate — turns a bump stop’s force-at-compression spec into a linear rate and combines it with the existing wheel rate, springs-in-parallel style.
Gearhead Labs Premium unlocks Cam Area / Time-Area — a true curtain-area time-area breathing index integrated across the full cam event.

Index = (Cam Duration × Target RPM) ÷ 720. A comparative index relating a cam’s duration to a target operating RPM — useful for comparing two cam/RPM combinations against each other, not as a standalone physical quantity.
Gearhead Labs Premium unlocks the Cam Motion Profile Analyzer — lift, velocity, and acceleration across the whole valve event in one table.

entries.definition: The inward or outward tilt of the wheel seen from the front; negative camber tilts the top of the wheel inward.

entries.description: Dynamic camber = static camber + (body roll × camber gain rate). Target: outer front tire near 0° dynamic camber for max contact patch. Camber gain rate depends on suspension geometry.
Timing change is normally stated in crankshaft degrees; the camshaft physically rotates at half crank speed.

entries.term: CAMSHAFT · Complete Cam Card / Valve Events
entries.description: Consolidates the four valve events, centerlines, LSA, duration and overlap at one measurement lift.
Duration must be compared at the same lift reference; advertised and .050-inch duration are not interchangeable.
Calculates duration, LSA, and overlap from cam timing events.
EVO and EVC are derived from exhaust duration and exhaust centerline using the same lift reference.
For a fixed-LSA cam, intake centerline is LSA minus installed advance. Lower centerline numbers indicate more advance.
IVC at a stated lift reference is derived from intake duration and intake centerline. Earlier IVC generally increases effective compression, all else equal.
LSA, intake centerline and exhaust centerline are related geometrically. Select the quantity to solve for.

Data Rate = Bits per Frame × Frames per Second. The actual bandwidth a set of CAN messages is consuming, useful for checking traffic load against the rated bitrate of the bus (commonly 500 kbps or 1 Mbps).
Gearhead Labs Premium unlocks Capacitive Reactance — the AC opposition a capacitor presents to current flow, feeding directly into Impedance and AC Power Factor.
Recommended CFM = (Displacement × RPM × VE) / 3456. For a single 4-barrel.

entries.definition: The fore-and-aft tilt of the steering axis seen from the side; positive caster tilts the top of the axis rearward.

entries.description: DIY caster measurement: turn the wheel to full lock each direction and read camber at each. Caster ≈ (camber difference / 2), normalized to a 20° sweep. Less precise than a caster gauge but useful without one.

entries.term: Caster Trail / Camber Gain in Turn
entries.description: More caster adds dynamic negative camber to the outside front wheel as you turn the wheel — "free" camber gain exactly when cornering. Camber Gain ≈ Caster × sin(steering angle). Higher caster helps mid-corner grip on the outside front tire.

inputs: Steering Angle (at this point in turn)

Gearhead Labs Premium unlocks CdA from Coast-Down Data — turns a measured coast-down time between two speeds into your real drag area (CdA), the inverse of the Free Aerodynamic Drag Force calculator.

Locates the CG laterally across the track width using left/right measured weights. Result is measured from the left tire contact centerline.
Locates the center of gravity along the wheelbase from the front axle using measured front and rear axle weights.
Gearhead Labs Premium unlocks Chassis/Frame Torsional Stiffness — twist angle and lb-ft per degree from a torsion-rig test.

Pro tree: all 3 ambers flash simultaneously, then green 0.4 sec later. Sportsman tree: ambers flash sequentially 0.5 sec apart, then green 0.5 sec after the last amber — giving more time to anticipate but requiring precise sequential timing.

entries.description: Fork ratio = distance from pivot to release-bearing contact ÷ pivot-to-pushrod distance. Geometry determines release travel and force.
Hydraulic force ratio is based on piston areas. A larger slave cylinder increases force and reduces slave travel for a given master-cylinder stroke.
A simplified pedal-effort estimate combining pedal leverage and hydraulic force multiplication.
Pedal ratio = pedal arm length ÷ pushrod attachment distance. Higher ratio increases release force at the expense of pedal travel.
Simplified release force estimate from pressure-plate load and release-lever ratio. Actual diaphragm-spring curves are nonlinear.
Simplified torque capacity = clamp load × friction coefficient × effective radius × friction surfaces.

entries.definition: The most torque a clutch can transmit without slipping, set by clamp load, friction coefficient, mean friction radius and the number of friction surfaces.

entries.description: Gearhead Labs Premium unlocks Coil Dwell & Spark Energy — models ignition coil primary charging as a standard RL circuit, showing stored spark energy at your actual dwell time.
k = G × d⁴ / (8 × n × D³) where G = 11,500,000 psi for steel
Gearhead Labs Premium unlocks Combined Axial + Bending Stress — peak fiber stresses and the yield safety factor of a bar or tube.

Gearhead Labs Premium unlocks Combined Slip — the slip-kinematics analog of the Free Friction Circle, showing how simultaneous braking/accelerating and cornering slip reduce each other’s available tire force.

Hydraulic Power Index = Fuel Flow × Rail Pressure. A comparative index for how much hydraulic work an injection system is doing — useful for comparing the relative demand of two rail-pressure/flow combinations against each other.

Efficiency = Ideal Temperature Rise ÷ Actual Temperature Rise. How close a real compressor gets to the ideal (isentropic) temperature rise for its pressure ratio — a lower efficiency means more waste heat for the same boost level.

Outlet Temp = Inlet Temp × [1 + (Pressure Ratio^0.2857 − 1) ÷ Efficiency]. The real (non-ideal) temperature rise across a turbo or supercharger compressor — the heat that an intercooler then has to remove before the air reaches the engine.

Pressure Ratio = Outlet Absolute Pressure ÷ Inlet Absolute Pressure. The actual compression a turbo or supercharger’s compressor is providing — the fundamental spec that drives compressor map selection and outlet temperature.
Gearhead Labs Premium unlocks Conduction Heat Transfer — Fourier’s Law for heat flow through a solid material, complementing the Free (convective) Heat Transfer calculator.
Gearhead Labs Premium unlocks Connecting Rod Angularity — the max rod angle and thrust-side loading behind every rod-ratio decision.
Control Error = Setpoint − Measured Value. The gap a closed-loop controller (a boost controller, idle control, or traction control) is actually trying to correct at this instant.

Gearhead Labs Premium unlocks Convection Heat Transfer — derives the convective coefficient itself from flow conditions (Dittus-Boelter), instead of requiring it as a raw input like the Free Heat Transfer calculator.
Slip % = (1 − Turbine RPM / Engine RPM) × 100. Street converters slip 2–5% at cruise; high-stall drag units slip 10–20%.

Coolant Flow = Heat Load ÷ (Specific Heat × Allowed Temperature Rise). The coolant mass flow needed to carry away a given heat load without the coolant itself rising more than the allowed temperature across the engine or radiator.
Interpolates a published ethylene-glycol/water reference table. Actual protection depends on the exact coolant formulation; use the manufacturer chart for service decisions.
Gearhead Labs Premium unlocks Cooling System Pressure & Boil Point — see your coolant mixture’s boiling point at your actual radiator cap rating, not just at sea-level atmospheric.

Analyzes four corner weights and reports total weight, front/rear distribution, left/right distribution and cross weight. For the oval-racing wedge/bite framing of this same data, see Cross Weight / Corner Balance.

Cornering Stiffness = Lateral Force ÷ Slip Angle. How much cornering force a tire generates per degree of slip angle in its linear (most predictable) response range — a stiffer tire builds grip faster as slip angle increases, up to the point it starts to saturate.

Gearhead Labs Premium unlocks Corrected Compressor Mass Flow & Speed — converts a measured flow and shaft speed to the SAE-corrected values your compressor map is actually plotted in, and stages them straight into the Turbo Compressor Map Builder.
Total ownership cost divided by miles driven. Useful for comparing vehicles, deciding whether to keep or replace, or setting mileage reimbursement rates.
Calculates the depth needed for a flat-head screw to sit flush. Depth = (Countersink Diameter / 2) / tan(included angle / 2). Standard angle is 82° (US) or 90° (metric/ISO).
Positive overlap means the journals physically intersect in side view — critical for stroker builds. Negative = no overlap, weaker crank.
Gearhead Labs Premium unlocks Crankcase Compression Ratio — the primary compression ratio of a crankcase-scavenged two-stroke.

entries.definition: In a crankcase-scavenged two-stroke engine, the ratio of the crankcase volume with the piston at top dead centre to the volume with it at bottom dead centre.
entries.distinctions: It describes the crankcase pumping that transfers the charge, not compression in the combustion chamber.

entries.term: CYLINDER HEAD / FLOW · CFM ↔ Velocity ↔ CSA
entries.description: Continuity relates volumetric flow, cross-sectional area and average velocity: Q = A·V. This is a volumetric relationship, so air density does not enter into it — density would only matter if converting to a mass flow rate. Use the same SOLVE FOR pattern used elsewhere in Gearhead Labs.

entries.description: Use the free single-point flow calculators to check individual numbers. Premium’s Cylinder Head Flow Curve builds the complete lift-vs-flow curve with charting — the full engineering problem, not just one point.

entries.term: CYLINDER HEAD / FLOW · Intake Port CFM
entries.description: Use the free CFM ↔ Velocity ↔ CSA calculator to establish the baseline relationship. Premium’s Intake Port CFM analyzes the complete intake-side flow picture.

entries.term: CYLINDER HEAD / FLOW · Intake Throat Diameter Sizing
entries.description: Gearhead Labs Premium unlocks Intake Throat Diameter Sizing — turns a target CFM and velocity straight into an actual throat diameter to size or machine to.

entries.term: CYLINDER HEAD / FLOW · Mach Index / Velocity
entries.description: Mach index is average velocity divided by estimated speed of sound. Treat it as an engineering indicator rather than an absolute universal limit.

entries.term: CYLINDER HEAD / FLOW · Port/Throat Area → HP Estimator
entries.description: Gearhead Labs Premium unlocks the Port/Throat Area → HP Estimator — find out whether your heads can flow enough to support your power target before you buy them.

entries.term: CYLINDER HEAD / FLOW · Port-to-Valve Area Ratio
entries.description: Compares entered port CSA with geometric valve-head area. There is no single correct ratio across all combinations.

entries.term: CYLINDER HEAD / FLOW · Required Port CSA
entries.description: Calculates area required to carry target flow at target average velocity. No single velocity is universally correct for every engine.

entries.term: CYLINDER HEAD / FLOW · Valve Throat Area
entries.description: Calculates throat area and throat percentage relative to the valve. It is a geometry descriptor, not a universal porting target.

Continuity relates volumetric flow, cross-sectional area and average velocity: Q = A·V. This is a volumetric relationship, so air density does not enter into it — density would only matter if converting to a mass flow rate. Use the same SOLVE FOR pattern used elsewhere in Gearhead Labs.
Gearhead Labs Premium unlocks Damper Velocity from Wheel Travel — converts a wheel-travel event into the shaft velocity a damper dyno plot is actually indexed against.

Gearhead Labs Premium unlocks Damping Coefficient from Target Ratio — reverse-solves the Free Damping Ratio relationship from physical wheel rate and corner weight, giving the actual shock valving spec instead of requiring it as an input.

Damping Ratio = Actual Damping Coefficient ÷ Critical Damping Coefficient. Where a shock or damper sits between undamped (oscillates freely, ratio 0) and critically damped (returns to rest with no overshoot, ratio 1) — most road and performance suspensions target somewhere well under 1.
Gearhead Labs Premium unlocks DC Fast-Charge Time — constant-current and constant-voltage taper charging time and energy, as an engineering estimate.

Level Difference = 20 × log₁₀(Amplitude Ratio). Converts a raw amplitude ratio (sound pressure, vibration amplitude, voltage) into the decibel scale actually used to describe how much louder or quieter one signal is than another.
Universal converter for any measurement — tape measures, calipers, blueprints, or CAD models. Not tied to any specific drill or bolt chart.

Deck clearance = block deck height − (half stroke + rod length + piston compression height). Positive result means the piston is below deck; negative means it is above deck.

DEF Consumption = Fuel Consumption × DEF Ratio. Diesel Exhaust Fluid is consumed by an SCR system at a rate roughly proportional to diesel fuel consumption — typically 2-3% of fuel volume for a modern SCR-equipped engine.
Estimate DEF consumption cost for a defined distance or operating interval.
Estimate distance or operating range from DEF tank capacity and DEF consumption rate.

A delay box adds a precise delay after you release the transbrake button, letting a driver with a very fast raw reaction consistently hit a target RT — legal in bracket racing (with class rules), illegal in most heads-up classes.

Calculates density altitude from field elevation, altimeter setting, temperature and dew point using the National Weather Service virtual-temperature method. Pressure and humidity therefore affect the result.
Estimates vehicle value year-over-year. New cars typically lose 20% in year 1, then roughly 10–15% per year after. Luxury and EVs often depreciate faster; trucks and Toyotas/Hondas slower.
Dew Point ≈ Temp − (100 − RH) / 5 with temperatures in °C (in °F the drop is 1.8 times as large). Low dew point (< 50°F) = dense, dry air = more power!

Enter your last 4 runs to calculate a suggested dial-in. Add a small cushion (0.01-0.03 sec) above your average to protect against breakout on a good run — but not so much that you leave time on the table.

AFR = Lambda × Diesel Stoichiometric AFR. Diesels run substantially leaner overall than gasoline engines (no throttle plate to limit airflow), so a diesel’s typical lambda range runs well above 1.0 even at high load.

Educational diesel air-fuel ratio and lambda converter (Lambda = AFR / stoichiometric AFR). Diesel engines normally operate lean except during transient or special operating conditions. For the reverse direction — lambda and stoich AFR to actual AFR — see Diesel AFR from Lambda.
Estimate brake mean effective pressure from power, RPM and displacement.
Calculate absolute manifold pressure ratio from boost and ambient pressure.
Estimate brake specific fuel consumption from fuel flow and brake horsepower. Lower is generally better at the same operating point.

Outlet Temp = Inlet Temp × [1 + (Pressure Ratio^0.2857 − 1) ÷ Efficiency]. The same isentropic compressor relationship used on gasoline turbos, applied to a diesel turbo’s typically higher pressure ratios — the heat a diesel’s (often larger) intercooler has to remove.
Translate fuel economy and diesel price into operating cost per mile and annual fuel expense.

EGR Flow = Total Intake Flow × EGR Fraction. How much exhaust gas is actually being recirculated back into the intake at a given EGR valve setting — diluting the intake charge to lower peak combustion temperature and reduce NOx formation.
Four-stroke CFM = CID × RPM × VE ÷ 3456. Mass flow = CFM × air density.
Compare current power demand with rated engine output.

Backpressure = Exhaust Manifold Pressure − Intake Manifold Pressure. A key diesel health check — a large positive differential means the turbine or exhaust system is unusually restrictive, costing power and fuel economy and increasing thermal stress on the engine.

Exhaust Flow = Airflow + Fuel Flow. Basic conservation of mass — everything that goes into the cylinder as air or fuel has to come back out as exhaust, the total flow the turbine and aftertreatment system actually have to handle.
Calculate MPG and fuel cost per mile from measured distance, fuel used and diesel price.
Estimate fuel mass and volume flow from power and BSFC.
Compare two fuel-economy levels over a defined mileage or operating interval.
Estimate annual fuel consumption and cost caused by engine idling.

Duration = Fuel Quantity ÷ Injector Flow Rate. How long an injector needs to stay open to deliver a target fuel quantity at its rated flow rate — the base timing figure an ECU’s injection strategy is built around.

Fuel per Cycle = Total Fuel Flow ÷ Engine Cycles per Minute. The actual fuel mass delivered across all cylinders in a single combustion cycle — the base quantity an injection strategy has to divide across however many injection events make up that cycle.
Four-stroke model: mg/injection × injections/cycle × cylinders × RPM/2 gives mg/min. It is converted to lb/hr and gal/hr using fuel density.

Injection Midpoint = Start of Injection + (Duration ÷ 2). A quick estimate of where an injection event is centered in crank angle — useful for comparing timing between two injection strategies without needing full injection-rate-shape data.
Estimate charge-air cooler effectiveness from compressor-out, cooler-out and ambient temperatures.
Combine fuel, labor and maintenance assumptions into a machine operating-cost estimate.
Estimate brake horsepower from fuel mass flow and assumed BSFC.
Compare engine output with machine mass.
Calculate torque from brake horsepower and RPM.

Pressure Ratio = Turbine Inlet Pressure ÷ Outlet Pressure. How much pressure drop the turbine itself is extracting energy from — the exhaust-side counterpart to the compressor’s intake-side pressure ratio.
Efficiency = Ideal Power ÷ Actual Power. How close a turbocharger’s real combined turbine-and-compressor performance gets to the theoretical ideal for the pressure ratios it’s operating at.
Compare compressor pressure ratio with charge-air temperature rise.

Gearhead Labs Premium unlocks Diffuser Angle / Expansion — ramp angle, area expansion ratio and ideal pressure recovery for an underbody diffuser.
Convert between miles, kilometers, feet, meters, yards.
How far you can go on remaining fuel. DTE = Remaining Fuel × MPG. Reserve tank is typically 1–2 gallons below "empty" warning.
Fractions are reduced; nearest-fraction tools use 1/64-inch increments.
Estimate fuel cost associated with regeneration events over an operating period.

Regen Interval = Soot Capacity ÷ Net Soot Accumulation Rate. How long a diesel particulate filter can run before it hits its soot load threshold and needs an active regeneration event to burn the accumulated soot off.

Soot Accumulation = (Generation Rate − Passive Regeneration Rate) × Time. The net soot actually building up in a diesel particulate filter, after subtracting whatever passive regeneration is already burning off during normal driving.
Gearhead Labs Premium unlocks Drag Coefficient — extracts Cd (and CdA) from a measured drag force, the reverse of the Free Aerodynamic Drag Force calculator.
Gearhead Labs Premium unlocks Drag / Downforce Tradeoff — compares two aero setups for downforce gained, drag and horsepower paid, and the grip it could buy.
Gearhead Labs Premium unlocks Drill Point Depth — the drill point length and the depth to the tip for any point angle.
Converts standard number, letter, and fractional drill designations. Input is normalized to uppercase and fractions are parsed when they are not already in the standard chart.
The RPM at which a driveshaft reaches resonance and can fail catastrophically. Always stay below 75% of critical speed.

entries.definition: The rotational speed at which a driveshaft's first bending natural frequency is excited, so it whirls and can fail.

entries.description: Gearhead Labs Premium unlocks Driveshaft Diameter Sizing — the strength-based sizing question the Free Driveshaft Critical Speed calculator doesn’t answer: the minimum diameter a solid shaft needs for a given torque and allowable stress.

Order Frequency = (Driveshaft RPM ÷ 60) × Order Number. The frequency a driveshaft imbalance or U-joint issue actually vibrates at — 1st order is once per driveshaft revolution, higher orders are harmonics of that.
Driveshaft RPM = Engine RPM / Transmission Gear Ratio
Gearhead Labs Premium unlocks Driveshaft Torque Capacity — the forward direction of Driveshaft Diameter Sizing’s torsion equation: the maximum torque an actual shaft or tube can carry.
Calculates wheel horsepower after drivetrain losses. Typical losses: Auto 18%, Manual 15%, Direct Drive 12%.

inputs: Drivetrain Loss Fraction (0.18 auto, 0.15 manual, 0.12 other)

entries.description: When two springs are in series: 1/k_total = 1/k1 + 1/k2. Then Wheel Rate = Series Rate × Motion Ratio².
Use the free Static Compression Ratio calculator to get your baseline CR. Premium’s Dynamic Compression Ratio accounts for cam timing to show what the engine actually sees.

entries.definition: The compression ratio counted from the moment the intake valve closes, using the piston position at intake valve closing instead of bottom dead centre.
entries.distinctions: It depends on the camshaft (intake valve closing point) and rod length as well as the static geometry.

related.note: The static ratio uses the full stroke; the dynamic ratio only the part after the intake valve closes.

entries.description: Dynamic Pressure = ½ × Air Density × Speed². The foundational “q” term behind every aerodynamic force calculation — drag, downforce, and lift all scale directly with this same dynamic pressure, just multiplied by a different shape-specific coefficient and area.
This is a simplified correction estimate. It is NOT a full SAE J1349 implementation because humidity and dry-air pressure inputs are not supplied.
Uses a volume-weighted ethanol balance. E85 content varies by season and fuel source, so enter the tested ethanol content when accuracy matters.

E85 Flow = Gasoline Flow × (Gasoline Energy Density ÷ E85 Energy Density). E85’s lower energy content means it takes more fuel flow to deliver the identical energy (and power) a gasoline calibration was flowing.
Shows how tire size changes your effective axle ratio. Get Stock/New Tire Diameter from Tire Size or Tire Size Comparison above.
Gearhead Labs Premium unlocks Electric Fan CFM Requirement — size an electric fan from your actual required heat rejection instead of guessing at a CFM rating.
Power = Voltage × Current. The basic power draw of any 12V accessory, from a fuel pump to a set of driving lights, given its operating voltage and current draw.

Density = (Absolute Pressure × 144) ÷ (53.35 × Absolute Temperature). The ideal-gas-law air density feeding directly into airflow and VE calculations — default inputs here match standard sea-level conditions.
CFM = (Displacement × RPM × VE) / 3456
Gearhead Labs Premium unlocks Engine Bobweight — the exact combined mass your balancer needs for a correct crank balance job.
Displacement = (π/4) × Bore² × Stroke × Cylinders

entries.definition: The total volume swept by all the pistons in one stroke: bore area times stroke times the number of cylinders.
entries.distinctions: It excludes the clearance (combustion chamber) volume.

entries.description: Gearhead Labs Premium unlocks Engine Mount Natural Frequency — the bounce frequency and static sag of a powertrain on its mounts.
Order Frequency = (RPM ÷ 60) × Order Number. The actual frequency of a specific vibration or noise order — for example, a V8’s dominant 4th-order firing frequency — at a given engine speed.
Back-calculates engine RPM from road speed, gear ratio, and tire size.
Strain = Change in Length ÷ Original Length. A dimensionless ratio describing how much a part stretches or compresses under load.
Rule of thumb: 60-foot ≈ ET × 0.120. Works well for stick-shift cars; automatics may vary.
Predicts new ET after a power increase or decrease. Formula: New ET = Old ET × (Old HP / New HP)^(1/3)
Predicts new ET after removing or adding weight. Formula: New ET = Old ET × (New Weight / Old Weight)^(1/3)
A consistent car is more valuable than a fast one in bracket racing. Standard deviation shows how tightly your ETs cluster — lower is better and lets you dial in tighter with less breakout risk.
Gearhead Labs Premium unlocks Euler Column Buckling — elastic critical load of a bar or tube with a slenderness check.
A simplified power-to-weight estimate for 0–60 mph. Launch traction, torque limits, gearing, battery output and thermal limits can materially change the result.

C-Rate = Battery Current ÷ Battery Capacity. A capacity-independent way of expressing how hard a battery is being discharged (or charged) — a 1C rate would fully discharge the pack in one hour, 2C in half an hour, and so on.

Coolant Flow = Heat Load ÷ (Coolant Heat Capacity × Allowed Temperature Rise). The coolant flow needed to remove a battery pack’s heat generation while keeping the pack’s temperature rise within a tight, battery-safe limit.
Battery current = electrical power ÷ battery voltage, adjusted for inverter efficiency.
Compares present usable capacity with original capacity to estimate capacity loss and remaining capacity percentage.
Battery energy = pack voltage × amp-hours. This is nominal stored energy; usable energy depends on the battery management system and state-of-charge limits.

Heat = Current² × Internal Resistance. Real I²R resistive heating inside the battery pack under load — the actual thermal load a battery cooling system has to remove, which grows with the SQUARE of current, not linearly.

Internal Resistance = Voltage Drop ÷ Current. Backs out a pack’s actual internal resistance from a measured voltage sag at a known current — rising internal resistance over time is one of the clearest signs of battery aging.

Peak Power = Pack Voltage × Peak Current ÷ 1000. The maximum electrical power a battery pack can actually deliver to the drive motor(s) at its rated peak current — the electrical-side ceiling on acceleration.
Pack Energy = Series Cells × Parallel Cells × Cell Voltage × Cell Ah ÷ 1000. The total usable energy a battery pack holds, built up directly from its cell count and individual cell specifications.

Loaded Voltage = Open-Circuit Voltage − (Current × Internal Resistance). How much a battery pack’s voltage actually drops under heavy current draw — real, unavoidable behavior of any battery with internal resistance, not a fault.
Charging cost = energy purchased × electricity price. Enter your actual utility or charging-network rate.

Charging Loss = Energy Drawn From Grid − Energy Actually Into Battery. The real energy wasted (mostly as heat) during a charging session — the gap between what the electric meter counts and what the battery actually gains.
Approximate charging time = energy added ÷ effective charger power. Actual charging curves taper near high state of charge.
Energy cost per mile = electricity price ÷ vehicle efficiency. This excludes time, maintenance, taxes and charging fees.

AC Output = DC Power × Conversion Efficiency. The actual AC power reaching the drive motor after inverter conversion losses — the counterpart calculation to Inverter Power Loss, framed around the delivered output instead of the loss.
Estimated range = usable battery energy × vehicle efficiency. Real-world range varies with speed, temperature, terrain, HVAC load and battery condition.

Energy Added = Charger Power × Charging Time × Charging Efficiency. The real energy that actually ends up in the battery after a charging session, accounting for AC-to-DC conversion losses during charging.
Calculates both miles per kWh and kWh per 100 miles from measured driving data.

HVAC Energy = HVAC Power × Driving Time. How much of the battery’s energy cabin heating or cooling actually consumes over a drive — a real, sometimes substantial draw on range, especially for resistive-heat cabin heating in cold weather.

Inverter Loss = DC Input Power − AC Output Power. The real power lost converting the battery’s DC power to the AC power a motor actually uses — modern inverters are highly efficient, but this loss still shows up as heat the inverter’s cooling system has to handle.

Efficiency = Mechanical Output Power ÷ Electrical Input Power. How much of the electrical power a drive motor actually converts to useful mechanical output — EV motors are dramatically more efficient at this than an internal combustion engine.
Mechanical power = torque × RPM. The result is motor shaft power before inverter, motor and drivetrain losses.
Reduction Ratio = Motor RPM ÷ Wheel RPM. Most EVs use a single fixed-ratio reduction gear (no multi-speed transmission) — this backs out that ratio from a matched motor and wheel speed reading.
Calculates approximate shaft torque from motor power and RPM. At very low RPM, real electric motors may be torque-limited rather than power-limited.
Pack Capacity = Cell Capacity × Parallel Strings. The pack’s total amp-hour rating — series-connected cells add voltage without changing this Ah figure, while parallel strings add capacity directly.

Power-to-weight estimate of quarter-mile ET and trap speed. ET = 5.825 x (weight / effective HP)^(1/3); trap = 234 x (effective HP / weight)^(1/3). These constants are empirical and ICE-derived, so a utilization factor is applied rather than assuming EV and ICE launch behave identically.

Stored energy = battery energy × current state of charge. This is a real-time snapshot — how much energy is in the pack right now at whatever the dash is showing. For the fixed usable-capacity ceiling of the pack itself, see EV Usable Battery Energy instead.

Adjusted Range = Baseline Range × (1 − Range Reduction Fraction). Cold temperatures reduce usable EV range through a combination of reduced battery efficiency and increased cabin heating load — this applies a known reduction fraction to a baseline range estimate.

Heuristic index = (vehicle weight ÷ reference weight) × (peak wheel torque ÷ reference torque) × driving-style factor. Reference values default to a typical mid-size ICE sedan. This is a comparative planning index, not a measured wear-rate model — compound, alignment, driving style and road surface all matter more than this index alone.

entries.description: Aero-limited top-speed estimate using available power, drag coefficient and frontal area. Rolling resistance and gearing are not included.

Cost per Mile = Energy per Mile × Electricity Price. Towing substantially raises an EV’s energy use per mile, directly raising the real cost per mile even though electricity itself is typically far cheaper per unit of energy than gasoline or diesel.

Towing Range = Baseline Range × (1 − Towing Penalty Fraction). Towing dramatically increases aerodynamic drag and rolling resistance, cutting EV range far more severely than the equivalent penalty on a gasoline vehicle’s range.

Usable energy = nominal battery energy × usable SOC fraction. This is a fixed characteristic of the pack and BMS — how much of the full pack the manufacturer allows you to actually use, buffering the top and bottom to protect battery life. For how much energy is available right now at a specific state-of-charge reading, see EV State of Charge Energy instead.

Wheel Torque = Motor Torque × Reduction Ratio × Drivetrain Efficiency. The actual torque reaching the wheels once the motor’s output is multiplied through the reduction gear — the real source of an EV’s characteristically strong, instant low-speed torque.
Uses established starting-point relationships for primary tube area/diameter and tuned primary length. This is a starting point, not a complete exhaust-system optimization.
Primary tube diameter based on HP per cylinder. Collector is typically 1.7× primary diameter. Oversized pipes hurt low-end torque.
Calculates how many average repairs you'd need to have during the warranty period to break even on its cost. If you expect fewer repairs than this, the warranty likely isn't worth it financially.
Factor of Safety = Material Strength ÷ Applied Stress. How much margin exists between a part's actual load and the point it would yield or fail.

Clamp Load = Torque ÷ (Nut Factor × Bolt Diameter). The actual clamping force a torque wrench setting produces in a bolted joint — the real number that holds a joint together, which torque alone only estimates through the nut factor.
Gearhead Labs Premium unlocks Fatigue Goodman Analysis — alternating and mean stress, Goodman safety factor and first-cycle yield check.
Gearhead Labs Premium unlocks Fatigue Soderberg Analysis — the conservative yield-based fatigue line and safety factor.
RPM = (SFM × 3.82) / Tool Diameter. Feed Rate = RPM × Number of Flutes × Chip Load. SFM (surface feet per minute) varies by material: mild steel ~80-100, aluminum ~300-600, stainless ~50-80.

Final Drive = Transmission Gear Ratio × Axle Ratio. Determines how much the engine is multiplied at the wheels.

entries.definition: The last gear reduction between the transmission output and the driven wheels, normally the differential's ring-and-pinion ratio.
entries.distinctions: The overall ratio in a given gear is the transmission gear ratio times the final drive ratio (times any transfer case or drop-box ratio).

entries.description: Gearhead Labs Premium unlocks the hydraulic Flow Coefficient (Cv) — the general liquid-valve Cv rating, alongside the Free engine-valve-specific Flow Coefficient calculator.

FMEP = IMEP − BMEP. The mean-effective-pressure equivalent of an engine’s internal friction and accessory losses — the gap between what the cylinder pressure could theoretically deliver and what actually reaches the crank as usable output.

Following Distance = Speed (converted to ft/sec) × Time Gap. The physical distance covered during a chosen time-gap rule (commonly 2-4 seconds) — the space actually needed to react to the vehicle ahead.
Quick conversion for reading blueprints, calipers, and drill charts that mix fractional and decimal measurements.

Decimal = Numerator ÷ Denominator. Millimeters = Decimal × 25.4. Enter a shop fraction (like 3/8) and get both its decimal-inch equivalent and its exact metric size together — useful for cross-referencing a fractional fastener or drill size against both a decimal caliper reading and a metric socket or drill bit.

entries.definition: The part of the indicated mean effective pressure lost to engine friction (and, in many definitions, pumping): IMEP minus BMEP.

entries.description: Gearhead Labs Premium unlocks Front/Rear Roll Stiffness Distribution — runs the Free Roll Stiffness formula for both axles in one pass, feeding straight into Roll Couple Distribution for the front/rear balance tuners actually act on.
Gearhead Labs Premium unlocks Frontal Area from Dimensions — a quick frontal-area estimate from width, height and an editable fill factor, ready to feed the drag and downforce calculators.

Efficiency = Electrical Output ÷ Fuel Chemical Energy Input. How much of the chemical energy in the hydrogen fuel a fuel cell stack actually converts to usable electrical power, with the rest lost mostly as heat and water.
Power = Hydrogen Mass Flow × Hydrogen Energy Content × Efficiency. The electrical power a hydrogen fuel cell stack produces from a given hydrogen consumption rate and stack efficiency.
Calculates MPG and L/100km from distance and fuel used.
Fuel Flow = Horsepower × BSFC. The actual fuel consumption rate an engine needs at a given power output and brake-specific fuel consumption.

New Flow = Known Flow × √(New Pressure ÷ Known Pressure). Injector flow scales with the square root of fuel pressure — the standard relationship for finding an injector’s actual flow rate at a fuel pressure different from its rated spec pressure.
Convert between lb/hr and cc/min injector flow ratings.
Injector Flow = (Target HP × BSFC) ÷ (Cylinder Count × Max Duty Cycle). The minimum flow rating each injector needs to support a horsepower target without running past a safe maximum duty cycle.

Calculates required injector flow rate at your chosen duty cycle. lb/hr = (HP × BSFC) / (injectors × duty cycle). A quick-estimate version of Fuel Injector Flow (per Injector) that also converts to cc/min.
Calculates frictional pressure loss with the Darcy-Weisbach equation. Add fittings separately if needed. Fuel properties and line roughness matter, so the defaults are only a gasoline starting point.
Calculates exact fuel required for a stint plus safety buffer. Running out of fuel on track costs far more time than carrying a little extra.
Estimate diesel consumption and fuel cost per acre from machine burn rate and field time.
Estimate fuel consumed and fuel cost per operating cycle.
Calculates pit stop count, fuel per stop, and laps per green-flag stint for oval races.
Measure fuel and fuel cost against tons moved or produced. Useful for heavy equipment and vocational work.
For returnless systems, fuel pressure should rise 1:1 with boost to maintain proper fuel flow.

Pump Capacity = Engine HP × BSFC × Safety Factor. The minimum fuel pump flow rating needed to support a horsepower target with margin for voltage sag, line loss, and headroom for future power increases.
Required pump volume flow from power, BSFC, fuel density, and capacity margin. Select a pump rated to deliver this flow at the required system pressure.
Calculates how much to slow down to achieve a target fuel saving percentage. Lift and coast, short-shift, and smooth throttle all contribute.

HP Capacity = Available Fuel Flow ÷ BSFC. The maximum horsepower a fuel system (pump plus injectors) can actually support at a given fuel flow rate and BSFC — the ceiling before running out of fuel supply, regardless of what the engine could otherwise make.
Fuse = load amps × 125% for continuous loads. Pick next standard size up. Never upsize a fuse to "fix" a blowing fuse — find the cause.

Calculates average G-force during the 60-foot trap. Formula: G = 2×d / (g×t²)
Calculates oil required for 2-stroke premix ratios.

GCWR Margin = Gross Combined Weight Rating − Actual Combined Weight. The margin left in the tow vehicle and trailer combination together — the single most important limit to respect when towing, since exceeding it stresses the whole drivetrain, brakes, and chassis together.

GCWR (Gross Combined Weight Rating) is the max weight of tow vehicle + trailer + all cargo/passengers/fluids combined. Exceeding it voids warranties and is genuinely dangerous — brakes and structure are only rated to that number.
Gearhead Labs Premium unlocks Gear Mesh Frequency — mesh, shaft and hunting-tooth frequencies of a gear pair.
Calculates vehicle speed from RPM, axle ratio, and tire diameter.
Maps out RPM landing points after each shift given your gear ratios and shift RPM. Ensures each shift keeps you in the power band (near or above peak torque RPM) for maximum acceleration.
Gearhead Labs Premium unlocks Gear Tooth Bending Stress — the classic Lewis equation screening check for gear-tooth root bending, alongside the Free general Bending Stress calculator.
Gearhead Labs Premium unlocks Gear Tooth Contact Stress — a simplified AGMA/Hertzian contact (pitting) stress screening check, the companion failure mode to Gear Tooth Bending Stress.
Each gear mesh loses ~1–2% power. Total efficiency = (per-stage efficiency)^stages. Heat is the enemy of transmission longevity.

Gearhead Labs Premium unlocks Gearbox Efficiency by Gear — runs the Free Gearbox Efficiency calculator’s own formula once per gear position, since different gears engage different numbers of gear meshes.
Calculates grains of water per pound of dry air using vapor pressure and barometric pressure. Lower grains generally indicate drier air.

Gearhead Labs Premium unlocks Ground Effect Estimate — an idealized underbody-venturi downforce estimate from the inlet and throat gaps, clearly labeled as an upper bound.

GVWR Margin = Gross Vehicle Weight Rating − Actual Vehicle Weight. How much more the tow vehicle itself (fully loaded, not counting the trailer) could weigh before exceeding its own single-vehicle weight rating.

Approximates conversions between Rockwell C (HRC), Brinell (HB), and Vickers (HV) hardness scales. These are empirical approximations valid roughly in the 20–65 HRC range — use ASTM E140 tables for precision work.

Harmonic Frequency = Base Frequency × Harmonic Number. Where the Nth harmonic of a fundamental vibration or noise actually falls — useful for tracking down a driveline boom or resonance that shows up at a multiple of a known base frequency.
Volume = π/4 × bore² × compressed thickness × 16.387 (converts in³ to cc). Essential for accurate compression ratio calculations.

Effectiveness = Actual Heat Transfer ÷ Maximum Possible Transfer. How close a radiator, intercooler, or oil cooler is getting to the theoretical best case set by the inlet temperatures and flow rates alone.
Heat Input = Fuel Mass per Cycle × Fuel Lower Heating Value. The chemical energy released in a single cylinder’s combustion event — the starting point for indicated-cycle thermodynamic analysis.

Heat Transfer Rate = Coefficient × Area × Temperature Difference. A basic convective heat transfer estimate — useful for a radiator core, heat shield, or any surface moving heat between two fluids or a fluid and the air.

When repairing stripped threads, the STI (Screw Thread Insert) drill is oversized specifically for the insert being used — always use the insert manufacturer's exact drill and tap, not a generic oversize.

Hitch Margin = Hitch Rated Tongue Capacity − Actual Tongue Weight. The real margin left on the hitch itself — a separate check from the tow vehicle’s overall payload, since a hitch is rated for tongue weight specifically, not total vehicle weight.

Force = system pressure × piston area (Pascal law). Extend stroke uses the full bore area; retract stroke uses the smaller annular area (bore area minus rod area), which is why a cylinder always pushes harder than it pulls at the same pressure.

Speed = flow rate ÷ piston area. Because the retract (annular) area is smaller than the full bore area, the same pump flow moves the rod faster on retract than on extend — the opposite of force, which is higher on extend. Force and speed trade off against each other at a fixed flow rate.

Pascal law: pressure is equal throughout a connected fluid system, so force scales with the ratio of piston areas — F₂ = F₁ × (A₂/A₁). This is how a hydraulic jack multiplies a small input force into a large output force, at the cost of the output piston moving a proportionally shorter distance for the same fluid volume.

Theoretical flow = displacement × RPM, converted from in³/min to gallons/min (231 in³ per gallon), then reduced by volumetric efficiency to account for internal slip. Gear pumps typically run 80-90% volumetric efficiency; piston pumps 90-98%.

Total displaced fluid volume = cylinder swept volume (bore area × stroke × number of cylinders) plus line volume (line cross-section × length), then increased by a safety margin for thermal expansion, entrained air and pump inlet requirements. Estimated peak radial squish velocity, evaluated at 15° BTDC (the commonly-cited point of peak squish flow) using an annular squish-band model with harmonic piston motion. Over 80 ft/sec risks detonation from overly fast mixture motion; 50–75 ft/sec is typical for street use, up to 100 ft/sec for race fuel.
Current = Starter Power ÷ (System Voltage × Efficiency). The real electrical current a starter motor pulls to deliver its rated mechanical power, accounting for motor efficiency losses.

All chamber, gasket and piston volumes are normalized to cc before calculation. CR = (swept volume + clearance volume) / clearance volume. Piston volume is entered as positive for dome volume (subtracts from clearance) and negative for a dish (adds to clearance).

entries.definition: The ratio of the cylinder volume with the piston at bottom dead centre to the volume with it at top dead centre, from the full swept volume plus the clearance volume (chamber, gasket, deck and piston dome or dish).
entries.distinctions: It is fixed by geometry. It is not the pressure measured on a compression gauge, and it is not the dynamic ratio, which starts compression only when the intake valve closes.

related.note: Measured in the crankcase of a two-stroke, not in the cylinder.
Cranking compression is a measured pressure (psi or bar), not a volume ratio.
The dynamic ratio uses only the stroke left after the intake valve closes, so it is always lower.

entries.description: Steering Ratio = Steering Wheel Angle ÷ Road Wheel Angle. How much steering wheel rotation it takes to turn the front wheels a given amount — a lower (numerically smaller) ratio means quicker, more direct steering response.

Blend Stoich AFR = 1 ÷ [(Fraction A ÷ Stoich A) + (Fraction B ÷ Stoich B)]. The effective stoichiometric ratio of a mixed fuel — like a gasoline/ethanol blend — accounting for each component’s own stoichiometric requirement.

Parasitic Power = Boost Power Output × Parasitic Fraction. The power a supercharger itself consumes (off the crank or a belt) just to produce its boost — real net gain is boost power output minus this parasitic draw.
Calculates supercharger RPM from engine RPM and pulley ratio.

Motion Ratio = Spring Travel ÷ Wheel Travel. Most suspension linkages move the spring less than they move the wheel — this ratio (usually under 1.0) is exactly what converts a chosen spring rate into the wheel rate that actually determines ride frequency.
Calculates a solid sway bar spring rate and its contribution to total roll stiffness. Larger diameter = much stiffer (4th power). Longer arm = softer.
Calculates tank volume in gallons from internal dimensions.

Tap Drill = Major Diameter − (Pitch × Engagement% × 1.299) for metric, or Major − (0.649519/TPI × Engagement%) for inch threads. Standard engagement is 75%, but 60–70% extends tap life significantly with only ~5% strength loss.

Tap Drill = Major Diameter − (Pitch × Engagement% × 1.299) for metric, or Major − (0.649519/TPI × Engagement%) for inch threads. Standard engagement is 75%, but 60–70% extends tap life significantly with only ~5% strength loss.
Convert between Fahrenheit, Celsius, Kelvin, and Rankine.

Temperature Rise = Heat Input ÷ (Mass × Specific Heat). How much a component heats up after absorbing a given amount of energy — for example, a brake rotor absorbing the kinetic energy from a single stop.
Estimates top speed purely from aero drag equilibrium. Actual speed may be limited by gearing. P = ½ρV³CdA

Expansion = Original Length × Coefficient of Thermal Expansion × Temperature Change. How much a part physically grows or shrinks over a temperature swing — exhaust tubing, a long bracket, or a chassis rail heat-cycling.

Gearhead Labs Premium unlocks Thin-Wall Hoop Stress — pressure hoop stress with a thick-wall (Lamé) check and yield safety factor.
Gearhead Labs Premium unlocks Thin-Wall Longitudinal Stress — closed-end axial stress and the combined von Mises check.

Calculates the actual thread engagement percentage produced by a given tap drill size. Metric formula: ((Major − Drill) / (1.299 × Pitch)) × 100.

Pitch (mm) = 25.4 / TPI. TPI = 25.4 / Pitch (mm). Useful for matching imperial and metric fasteners or identifying an unknown thread.
Gearhead Labs Premium unlocks Thread Stripping Strength — FED-STD-H28 shear areas and the weakest link: bolt, bolt thread or nut thread.

Sizes the bore from actual airflow demand rather than a horsepower rule. CFM = CID x RPM x VE / 3456, required area = CFM x 144 / (velocity x 60), bore = 2*sqrt(A/pi). Factory throttle bodies typically run 150-200 ft/sec at peak; 175 is a sound starting target.
Solve for any of the three variables.
Calculates the arc length on harmonic balancer for a given degree of advance.

Fitting taller tires effectively raises your final drive and reduces usable crawl ratio. Tire factor = fitted diameter / stock diameter; adjusted crawl ratio = raw crawl ratio / tire factor. Use the Crawl Ratio calculator first if you need the raw figure.
Gearhead Labs Premium unlocks Tire Contact Patch Pressure & Area — the standard load-over-pressure footprint estimate, with no existing contact-patch calculator today.
Gearhead Labs Premium unlocks Tire Deflection — the straightforward load/spring-rate relationship for vertical tire compliance, the reverse direction of Tire Vertical Stiffness.
Models linear tire falloff from two reference lap times. Identifies when degradation becomes critical and total time loss over a stint.

Combined Demand = √(Longitudinal G² + Lateral G²). A tire has one finite total grip budget shared between braking/acceleration and cornering — this shows the real combined demand when both happen at once, which is always more than either alone.

Gearhead Labs Premium unlocks Tire Heat Generation — carries rolling-resistance power forward into accumulated heat energy and an adiabatic temperature-rise estimate, beyond Tire Rolling Resistance’s force/power alone.
Uses Gay-Lussac's Law (P₁/T₁ = P₂/T₂) to calculate hot tire pressure from cold inflation. Set cold pressure knowing your expected operating temperature.
Gearhead Labs Premium unlocks Tire Rolling Resistance — the universal, non-towing version of the Free Towing Rolling Resistance calculator’s same physics.

Frequency = (Speed converted to in/sec) ÷ Tire Circumference. How many times per second a tire is actually rotating at a given road speed — the base frequency behind a wheel-speed-related vibration or wheel balance diagnosis.

Decodes metric tire size into overall diameter, circumference, and revolutions per mile. Overall diameter = wheel diameter + 2 × sidewall height. Comparing an old size against a new one? Use Tire Size Comparison instead — it runs this same math for both sizes side by side and shows the speedometer and gearing effect of the change.

Runs the same decode as Tire Size for two tires at once and shows what actually changes: diameter delta, ground-clearance change, and how far off your speedometer reads at an indicated 60 mph. For the gear-ratio and full speedometer-calibration math using these diameters directly, continue to Effective Gear Ratio (Tires) or Speedometer Calibration.

Slip Angle = arctan(Lateral Velocity ÷ Longitudinal Velocity). The angle between where a tire is actually pointed and the direction it’s actually traveling — tires generate cornering force precisely BECAUSE of this angle, not despite it.
Gearhead Labs Premium unlocks Tire Slip Ratio — the standard SAE longitudinal slip percentage, a distinct quantity from the Free Slip Angle calculator’s lateral angle.
Stagger = right circumference − left circumference. Used in oval racing to help the car turn left. More stagger = more left-turn tendency.
Read tire temps across 3 points (inside/center/outside) per corner. Center hottest = over-inflated. Outside hottest = negative camber needed. Huge L/R spread = setup imbalance.
Gearhead Labs Premium unlocks Tire Vertical Stiffness — the vertical (ride) spring-rate axis, distinct from the Free Cornering Stiffness calculator’s lateral axis.

entries.definition: The angle of the wheels relative to the vehicle centreline seen from above: toe-in when the fronts of the tyres point towards each other, toe-out when they point apart.

entries.description: For symmetric toe, per-wheel toe angle = asin(total toe distance ÷ (2 × tire diameter)). Positive front-minus-rear distance is toe-out; negative is toe-in.
Tongue weight should be 10-15% of total loaded trailer weight. Too little causes sway; too much overloads the tow vehicle's rear axle and hitch receiver. Weigh it — don't guess.

Tongue Weight % = Tongue Weight ÷ Loaded Trailer Weight. The single most important towing stability number — too little and the trailer sways, too much and it overloads the hitch and rear axle; 10-15% is the widely-cited healthy range for a conventional trailer.
Gearhead Labs Premium unlocks Tool Deflection — tip deflection, stiffness and stress of a cutting tool as a cantilever.
Gearhead Labs Premium unlocks Tool Life — Taylor tool life, the speed for a target life and the cost of running faster.

entries.definition: For a limited-slip differential, the largest ratio of torque between the high-traction and low-traction wheels that it can sustain before the wheels slip relative to each other.

entries.description: Use the free Converter Slip % calculator to establish the baseline. Premium’s Torque Converter Stall Speed analyzes the complete stall-speed tuning problem.

entries.definition: The engine speed reached with the converter output held stationary at full throttle, set by the converter design and the engine torque.
entries.distinctions: Flash stall (on a launch) and brake stall (against the brakes) are measured differently and differ.

entries.description: Torque = (HP × 5252) / RPM
When using a torque wrench extension, set the wrench LOWER than target. Setting = Desired × (L / (L + E)). E = extension length, L = wrench length from drive to grip.
Gearhead Labs Premium unlocks Torsional Resonance Speed — the speed at which an excitation order meets a torsional natural frequency.
Torsional shear stress = Torque ÷ Polar Section Modulus. The peak shear stress at the outer surface of a shaft or tube under a twisting load.
Adds up depreciation, fuel, insurance, and maintenance over your ownership period — the real cost of owning a car beyond just the purchase price and loan payment.
Gearhead Labs Premium unlocks the Total Timing vs RPM/Load Helper — interpolates total ignition timing from your own base-timing and mechanical-advance curve points.

Remaining Payload = Payload Rating − People/Cargo Weight − Tongue Weight. Tongue weight rides on the tow vehicle, not the trailer, so it counts directly against the truck’s own payload rating alongside passengers and cargo.

Kinetic Energy = Combined Weight × Speed² ÷ 64.348. The full combined rig’s kinetic energy that the tow vehicle’s brakes (and whatever trailer brakes are helping) have to dissipate in a stop — dramatically more than the tow vehicle alone would generate at the same speed.
Towing Range = Fuel Capacity × Towing MPG. Real achievable range on a full tank while towing — using towing MPG here instead of unloaded MPG is what keeps fuel-stop planning realistic on a long tow.

Grade Power = Combined Weight × Grade × Speed ÷ 375. The power just to overcome gravity on an incline at a target speed — on top of (not instead of) the power already needed to overcome rolling resistance and aero drag at that same speed.

Grade Speed = Available Grade Horsepower × 375 ÷ (Combined Weight × Grade). The top speed a given amount of power (set aside purely for climbing) can sustain on a grade — the reverse of the Grade Power calculation, isolating gravity’s effect alone.

Towing MPG = Baseline MPG × (1 − Penalty Fraction). Aerodynamic drag and rolling resistance from a large trailer routinely cut fuel economy 30-50% — a real, substantial penalty worth planning trip fuel and range around rather than assuming unloaded MPG.

Rolling Resistance Force = Combined Weight × Rolling Resistance Coefficient. The steady force resisting motion from tire deformation alone, before adding aerodynamic drag or grade — a real, constant power draw that scales directly with total towed weight.

Measures ride height change front and rear when hitching up. A weight-distribution hitch should restore front ride height to within ~1 inch of unloaded, keeping steering weight and headlight aim correct.

Trip Fuel Cost = Trip Miles ÷ Towing MPG × Fuel Price. The real fuel budget for a towing trip, using the reduced towing MPG rather than the vehicle’s unloaded rating — planning a trip around unloaded MPG would badly underestimate the actual cost.

Wheel Torque = Engine Torque × Overall Gear Ratio × Drivetrain Efficiency. The real torque reaching the wheels once engine torque is multiplied through the transmission gear and axle ratio together — why a low gear feels so much stronger when towing up a grade.
